deep.reconstruction:
This page continues §1 of Riemann's Inaugural Dissertation, 'Grundlagen für eine allgemeine Theorie der Functionen einer veränderlichen complexen Grösse' (Göttingen 1851). The previous page carries that title in the form 'Über Functionen einer veränderlichen complexen Grösse'. The wording matches the printed §1 almost word for word, so the folio is a draft or fair copy of the dissertation's opening.

There is no computation on this page. The argument runs as follows.

(a) A dependence w = f(z) may be given by a mathematical law: a fixed sequence of 'Grössenoperationen' (analytic operations) yielding w from z.

(b) Earlier usage restricted 'one law on a whole interval' to a special class, Euler's functiones continuae. Newer work (implicitly Fourier and Dirichlet, 1822–1829) showed that analytic expressions exist that represent every continuous function on a given interval.

(c) Hence, for real z, defining w as an arbitrary dependence or as one fixed by analytic operations is the same thing. 'Beide Begriffe sind ... congruent.'

(d) This changes when z may take complex values z = x + yi, with i = sqrt(-1).

(e) Setup for the next page: let z = x+yi and z+dz = x+yi+dx+dy·i be infinitely close values of z. Let them correspond to w = u+vi and w+dw = u+vi+du+dv·i.

On the following page Riemann writes dz = ε e^{iφ} and expands dw/dz as
½(u_x+v_y) + ½(v_x−u_y)i + ½[(u_x−v_y) + (v_x+u_y)i]·e^{−2iφ}.
The quotient is therefore independent of the direction φ exactly when u_x = v_y and u_y = −v_x. This is the Cauchy–Riemann condition, which becomes his definition of a function of a complex variable. The present page only motivates that step and sets the notation.
errors: The claim that every continuous function on an interval is representable by an analytic expression was not proved in 1851 in the generality stated. Dirichlet's 1829 Fourier-series theorem required piecewise monotonicity (finitely many maxima and minima). Fourier series of some continuous functions in fact diverge (du Bois-Reymond 1876). The statement becomes rigorously true via Weierstrass's approximation theorem (1885): every continuous function is the sum of a uniformly convergent series of polynomials. This is an overstatement typical of the period, not a computational slip.

results.what: Equivalence, for real variables, of 'arbitrary (Dirichlet) function' and 'function given by an analytic expression', based on representability of continuous functions.
results.modern_name: Dirichlet function concept; Fourier series representation (later Weierstrass approximation theorem)
results.usually_credited_to: Fourier (1822), Dirichlet (1829/1837); rigorous general form Weierstrass (1885)

results.what: Motivation that complex-analytic dependence is more restrictive than arbitrary dependence; setup with z=x+yi, w=u+vi and differentials, leading to the Cauchy–Riemann definition.
results.modern_name: Definition of holomorphic function via direction-independence of dw/dz (Cauchy–Riemann equations)
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann's 1851 dissertation (equations earlier in d'Alembert, Euler, Cauchy)

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a draft or fair copy of the opening of Riemann's published 1851 dissertation, matching the printed text nearly verbatim. Nothing on it is new.

checkable.asserts: du + i·dv = A·dz + B·conj(dz), which is the decomposition used on the next page (should print 0).

transcription_corrections: The machine transcription is essentially correct against the image.
Line 13 of the manuscript reads 'willkührlich angenommene'. The printed dissertation has 'willkürlich gegebene', which is a draft-versus-print variant, not a transcription error.
The image spells 'definirt' and 'giebt' in the period orthography; the transcription keeps both correctly.
